title: Tell me about a time you took ownership beyond your role
prompt: Tell me about a time you took ownership of a problem that wasn't really yours to solve — something outside your assigned role or team. What made you step in, what did you do, and how did it turn out?
blurb: Ownership: did the candidate act like the problem was theirs — end to end — or wait for someone else to own it?

rubric.label: Situation & stakes
rubric.description: Sets up a concrete situation with enough context to judge why the problem mattered and why it was ambiguous who owned it.

rubric.label: Why they owned it
rubric.description: Explains what pulled them in — customer impact, a gap no one was filling, a risk they saw — rather than being told to. Shows the decision to step up was theirs.

rubric.label: Specific actions (I not we)
rubric.description: Describes the concrete steps THEY personally took, including navigating the fact that it wasn't their remit, without excessive 'we'.

rubric.label: Result & quantified impact
rubric.description: States a measurable outcome and ties it to their intervention — incident resolved, metric moved, launch unblocked.

rubric.label: Reflection & judgment
rubric.description: Shows awareness of when stepping in is right vs overstepping; what they learned about ownership and follow-through.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Answer is structured (roughly STAR), concise, and easy to follow under follow-up probing.

reference.scenario: The candidate should recall a moment where a problem fell through the cracks between teams or roles — a broken build no one owned, a customer escalation outside their area, a launch blocked by a dependency team, a data-quality issue upstream — and they chose to drive it to resolution rather than route it away or wait. Strong answers show they owned the outcome, not just their slice.
model_points: Situation: a real gap where ownership was genuinely unclear — cross-team seam, on-call surprise, an orphaned system — with stakes (customers affected, revenue, a deadline at risk).
Task: what they personally decided the outcome needed to be, and why they felt accountable despite it not being their job.
Action: concrete steps — diagnosed the issue, pulled in the right people, made or drove a decision, filled the gap themselves, and communicated status up and across.
Action: navigated the org reality — got buy-in or forgiveness, avoided stepping on the actual owner, handed it back cleanly once stable.
Result: quantified outcome (incident resolved in X, launch shipped on time, defect rate down Y%, cost avoided) attributed to their intervention.
Reflection: recognized ownership as owning the result end-to-end; also learned where the line is between initiative and overstepping, and set up a durable owner so it wouldn't recur.

probes.trigger: candidate stays in 'we' / describes team effort
probes.question: What specifically did YOU do here, versus what the rest of the team did? Walk me through your individual contribution.
How did you know it worked? What actually changed — a metric, a timeline, an incident count?
How did you handle the fact that this wasn't your job — did the actual owner or their manager know? How did you avoid stepping on toes?

probes.trigger: problem was solved but recurred / no handoff
probes.question: After you fixed it, who owned it going forward? How did you make sure it didn't just land back on you or fall through again?

probes.trigger: vague on decision to step in
probes.question: At the moment you noticed this, what were your options? Why step in yourself instead of escalating or flagging it?

red_flags: Only ever says 'we' and never isolates a personal action or decision.
'Took ownership' means they just complained loudly or escalated — no follow-through to resolution.
No result, or a result with no connection to what they did.
Overstepped recklessly — trampled the real owner, created conflict, no coordination — and shows no awareness of it.
Blames the org or other teams for the gap and frames themselves as the lone hero with no reflection.
Story is hypothetical or so generic it could describe anyone.
follow_ups: How much time did this take, and what did you deprioritize to do it? Was that the right trade?
How did your manager react to you spending time outside your lane?
Would you do it again the same way? What would you change?
Have you ever decided NOT to step into something that wasn't yours? How did you make that call?
reference.exemplar_answer: Situation: 'Our checkout service started throwing 5xxs at 2am. I was on the payments team, but the root cause was an upstream identity service owned by another team with no one on call that night, and customers couldn't pay.' Task: 'I decided the priority was stopping the customer bleeding, even though the failing service wasn't mine.' Action: 'I traced it to a bad config push on identity, paged their EM, and while waiting I shipped a temporary fallback in our service to degrade gracefully instead of hard-failing. I set up an incident channel, posted 15-minute updates to leadership, and once identity rolled back their change I verified recovery and handed the incident back.' Result: 'We cut the outage from a projected multi-hour event to 40 minutes, roughly $X in payments recovered, and zero data loss.' Reflection: 'Afterward I wrote the postmortem and pushed for cross-team on-call coverage and a graceful-degradation pattern so this class of failure wouldn't need a hero next time. I learned ownership means owning the outcome — but also handing it back with a durable fix rather than becoming the permanent owner by accident.'

interviewer_notes: Run this STAR-style. Let them tell the story, then probe hard on I-vs-we — this is the #1 signal for ownership and candidates default to 'we'. If they never quantify, push once for a metric or a concrete before/after. Distinguish real ownership (drove to a durable outcome) from noise (escalated, complained, or heroically overstepped without coordination). Senior-flavored maturity shows in the reflection: knowing when NOT to step in, and setting up a lasting owner. Reserve a probe for the handoff — did the fix stick, or did they just absorb someone else's job?
